claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a modest, homogeneously distributed manganese content.
Manganese preferentially dissolves from Q235 steel during molten-salt exposure at about 700 °C.
Preferential manganese dissolution produces a manganese-rich interfacial layer on Q235 steel.
The proposed manganese-rich interfacial layer is likely MnF2.
The manganese-rich interfacial layer buffers local redox conditions in the molten salt.
Manganese-mediated redox buffering reduces the thermodynamic drive and rate of iron dissolution or oxidation.
Suppressing iron dissolution through the proposed manganese buffer preserves the overall corrosion resistance of Q235 steel.
The standard Gibbs free energy of formation of manganese fluoride is lower than that of iron fluoride.
A Cr-Mn-Fe-Ni high-entropy alloy exposed to FLiBe at 700 °C exhibited rapid manganese dissolution into the salt.
Inert-atmosphere annealing can partially deplete or redistribute near-surface manganese in Q235 steel.
The proposed mechanism is operative under aggressive high-temperature molten-salt conditions near 700 °C.
The proposed mechanism does not operate at room temperature or in non-salt environments.
As-received Q235 steel will lose less mass than surface-Mn-depleted or Mn-redistributed Q235 steel under otherwise identical FLiBe exposure.
As-received Q235 steel will release less iron than surface-Mn-depleted or Mn-redistributed Q235 steel during FLiBe exposure.
Salt exposed to as-received Q235 steel will contain more manganese than salt exposed to surface-Mn-depleted Q235 steel.
Salt exposed to as-received Q235 steel will contain less iron than salt exposed to surface-Mn-depleted Q235 steel.
Equivalent mass loss, iron dissolution, and interfacial-layer formation in as-received and Mn-depleted specimens would falsify the proposed manganese-buffer mechanism.
